place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 外门后院 · 柴堆
place.en: Chending Temple · Behind the outer court · the woodpile

setup.zh: 九月十七，入门第八天。夜里，你照旧坐在外门后院的柴堆上：吹呴呼吸，吐故纳新。
setup.en: The seventeenth of the ninth month, your eighth day. At night you sit on the woodpile behind the outer court as always: blow and breathe out, draw and breathe in.

recap.zh: 九月十七夜里，你的气在身子里转了一个圈——一夜通了小周天。银月说：三道关，她替你凿了两道半。「你是漏勺。本王是补锅匠。」
recap.en: The night of the seventeenth, your qi went round your body in one circle — the small circuit, open in a single night. Yinyue said she had chiselled two and a half of the three gates for you. "You're a skimmer. I'm the tinker."

zh: 一股暖，顺着脊梁骨往上走——一节，一节。
en: A warmth climbs the spine — one joint, then the next.
"Three gates. I chiselled two and a half."

story.zh:
九月十七，入门第八天。

那一夜没有月亮，天上一层薄云，云后头透着一点星光，灰蒙蒙的。后院的柴堆黑沉沉的，墙根底下的蛐蛐叫得有气无力，大约也快到了该歇的时候。小满照旧爬上去，盘腿坐好，把木牌从衣领里掏出来，贴着胸口放着，闭上眼睛。

吹呴呼吸，吐故纳新。
story.en:
The seventeenth of the ninth month, his eighth day in the sect.

That night there was no moon, only a thin layer of cloud with a little starlight behind it, grey and dim. The woodpile in the back court loomed black; the crickets at the foot of the wall chirped half-heartedly, their season nearly done. Xiaoman climbed up as usual, sat cross-legged, drew the token from his collar and laid it against his chest, and closed his eyes.

Blow and breathe out, draw and breathe in; spit out the old, take in the new.

exits.means: breathes as the scroll says, sinks the mind down

story.zh:
吸进第一口气，他便觉出不一样来。

那口气是凉的，清的，像他家屋后那口井里刚打上来的水，从鼻子里进去，顺着喉咙往下流，一直流进肚子里。往常这口气流到胸口，便散了，像一瓢水泼进沙地，渗得无影无踪。这一回它没有散，它一直往下流，流过胸口，流过肚脐，流进肚脐底下三寸，一个他从来不知道有的地方——那里原来有一片湖。

那片湖是干的，冷的，湖底裂着一道一道的口子，像大旱年份的水田。那口凉气流进去，湖底便「滋」的一声，像烧红的铁淬了水。他吓了一跳，差点睁开眼睛，却听见胸口的木牌里，有一个极轻极轻的声音，道：「……别动。」

他便不动。

第二口气流进去，湖底湿了一片。第三口，湿了一大片。第四口，第五口，第十口，那片湖一点一点地涨起来，涨到半满，湖面上忽然**亮了**。

先是一点暖，像有人在湖心点了一盏灯。那盏灯起先只有豆粒大，一明一暗，跟他家灶间那盏掐短了芯子的油灯一模一样；烧着烧着，越烧越旺，暖意一圈一圈地荡开去，荡到他的腰，荡到他的腿，荡到他的指头尖。他还没来得及害怕，那股暖竟自己动了起来。

它冲出小腹，往下一沉，绕到后头，顺着脊梁骨的最底下一节，一节一节往上钻，像一条火做的小蛇。钻到后腰，撞上了一道门——他觉出那是一道门，硬邦邦的，冷冰冰的，横在脊梁骨里。可那小蛇撞上去，那门竟是开着的，门轴上还带着一点刚凿过的毛刺，小蛇一扭身，便钻过去了。

钻到后背正中，又是一道门。也是开着的。

钻到后脑勺，第三道门。这一道门，只开了一半。

那小蛇撞上去，撞了一下，没撞开，缩了回来。小满只觉得后脑勺像给人拿木槌敲了一记，眼前金星乱冒，那股暖在后脑勺底下打着转，一下一下地撞，撞一下，他的头便疼一下，疼得他牙根发酸。他咬紧了牙，心里却不知怎的，想起了他爹拉弓的样子——

先看风，后看鹿。拉满了，不忙着松手。等风歇一口气。

他便不撞了。他让那股暖在门后头停着，停着，一口气吸进来，慢慢地沉下去，再慢慢地吐出来。吸，沉，吐。一口，两口，三口。等到第九口气吐尽，后脑勺里那一下疼，忽然歇了一歇，像风停了一瞬——

他一口气吸到底，那股暖跟着这口气，一头撞了上去。

只听得脑中「轰」的一声，他眼前一白，像大晴天里抬头看了一眼日头。那股暖撞开了门，冲上头顶，在头顶上打了个转，翻将过来，顺着额头、顺着鼻梁、顺着喉咙、顺着胸口一路往下，哗啦啦地，像一道开了闸的水渠，落回肚脐底下，稳稳地停住了。

恰好是一个圈。

他睁开眼来。

天上还是那层薄云，柴堆还是那个柴堆，可看出去的东西，全都不一样了。院墙上每一道砖缝，他看得清清楚楚；墙根底下那只蛐蛐翅膀上的纹路，他看得清清楚楚；三间房外，孙二狗在梦里嘟囔「娘，我不吃糠」，他听得明明白白；隔壁伙房里明天早饭的咸菜是隔夜的，还有一缸米给耗子啃了一个角，他也闻了出来。

他坐在柴堆上，大气也不敢出，生怕一喘气，这一切便又没了。

胸口的木牌烫得像一块刚出锅的烙饼。

一只半透明的小银狐从木牌里钻了出来，蹲在他膝盖上。它打了个哈欠，眼皮耷拉着，一脸没睡够的模样，道：「……通了？」

小满结结巴巴地道：「通、通了！银月，我一夜就——就——」

它道：「知道。本王算好的。」

小满一怔：「……算好的？」

银月又打了个哈欠：「你以为这一年，你是白蹲的？」

小满愣住了。他张着嘴想了半天，道：「……是那颗洗髓丹？」

银月道：「洗髓丹，是洗烟囱。你那一身经脉，堵得跟你家灶间那根烟囱似的——十三年的烟火渣滓，吃糠咽菜吃出来的，一泡，全冲出来了。你还记得那盆水么？黑得能写字。」

小满点点头。那盆水他娘刷了一早上，一句也没问。

「可烟囱洗干净了，门还锁着。」银月道，「你身子里有三道门，一道比一道紧。你自己撞，照你那个撞法，撞到三十岁也撞不开，撞开了，脑袋也撞傻了。所以本王睡在你心口——」

它说着抬起一只爪子，在他后腰上点了一下，后背正中点了一下，后脑勺又点了一下，道：「尾闾，夹脊，玉枕。三道关。每天夜里，趁你吐纳的时候，拿本王的气，替你一点一点地凿。本王凿了两道半。最后那半道，得你自己撞——本王替你撞，你这辈子都不知道门是怎么开的。」

小满张着嘴，半天说不出话来。

他想起在家里那一冬，每天夜里坐在柴垛上吐纳，什么都没有，小腹底下一口枯井。他以为什么都没有。他想起每天夜里吐纳完了，把木牌捧在手心里报账，报完了，木牌总是暖的。他以为那是他手心焐热的。

三百多个夜里，他坐在柴垛上，只道自己是一口枯井，什么都没有；原来一直有人在井底下，替他挖。

过了好一阵，他才道：「……所以我不是天才。」

银月道：「你是漏勺。本王是补锅匠。」

小满「噗」地笑出了声，笑到一半，却笑不下去了。他这才看清了它。

它比上回薄了。上回在讲堂上，它只出了一个声，没露面；再上回，是去年秋天，它钻进木牌那一夜，薄得像一层纸，月光能从它身上透过去。今天没有月亮，只有一点星光，那点星光竟也能从它身上透过去，透过它的身子，他看得见后头的柴堆，看得见柴堆上一根一根的松木。它那一条尾巴垂着，垂在他膝盖上，连尖儿都不翘了，尾根上那八道断口，颜色比去年深了。

他道：「……那你呢？你凿了一年，你——」

银月把脸扭开，道：「本王是妖王。凿几道门，算什么。」

小满不说话，只看着它。

它不看他，望着院墙外头黑沉沉的山，过了一会儿，又低声道：「……就是要多睡几天。」

它顿了一顿，又回过头来瞥了他一眼，道：「还有，你那一年，每天夜里跟本王报账。今天挑了几担水，明天马小宝吃了几块糕。吵死了。」

小满脸上一红：「你……都听见了？」

银月道：「本王睡着，又不是聋了。」

它说完这句，便不再说了。小满也不再说了。柴堆底下的蛐蛐叫了两声，又歇了。他想起去年秋天，木牌凉凉的，没有暖，他在柴垛上坐到月亮落下去。那一夜，他说的是一句什么话，他记得清清楚楚。

它说了挑水，说了马小宝的糕，偏偏没提那一句。他张了张嘴，想问，终于没有问。
story.en:
With the first breath he felt the difference.

That breath was cool and clear, like water just drawn from the well behind his house. It went in at his nose and down his throat, all the way into his belly. Always before, a breath like that had scattered once it reached his chest, like a ladle of water thrown on sand and soaked away without a trace. This time it did not scatter. It kept flowing down, past his chest, past his navel, into a place three inches below the navel that he had never known was there — and there, it turned out, was a lake.

The lake was dry and cold, its bed cracked in seams like a paddy in a drought year. The cool breath flowed in and the lakebed hissed, like red-hot iron quenched in water. He jumped and nearly opened his eyes, but from the token on his chest came a very, very faint voice: "…Don't move."

So he didn't move.

The second breath flowed in, and a patch of the lakebed grew wet. The third, a large patch. The fourth, the fifth, the tenth — the lake rose bit by bit, and when it was half full, its surface suddenly **lit**.

First a little warmth, as if someone had lit a lamp in the middle of the lake. The lamp was no bigger than a bean at first, flickering, exactly like the short-wicked oil lamp in his family's kitchen; but it burned brighter and brighter, and the warmth spread in rings — to his waist, his legs, the tips of his fingers. Before he had time to be afraid, the warmth began to move of its own accord.

It rushed out of his belly, sank, curled round to the back and bored up the spine from its very lowest joint, one joint at a time, like a little snake made of fire. At the small of his back it met a gate — he could feel it was a gate, hard and cold, set across his spine. But when the little snake struck it, the gate was open, the hinge still rough with fresh chisel marks, and the snake twisted and was through.

Halfway up his back, a second gate. Open too.

At the back of his head, a third. This one stood only half open.

The little snake struck it, didn't get through, and recoiled. Xiaoman felt as if someone had hit the back of his skull with a wooden mallet; stars burst before his eyes. The warmth circled under the back of his head, butting and butting; each butt made his head ache, till his teeth throbbed. He clenched them — and somehow, he thought of his father drawing the bow:

Watch the wind first, then the deer. Draw it full, and don't hurry to let go. Wait for the wind to catch its breath.

So he stopped butting. He let the warmth rest behind the gate, rest; drew in a breath, sank it slowly, let it slowly out. In, sink, out. One breath, two, three. When the ninth breath was spent, the ache at the back of his head paused for an instant, the way wind stops for a moment —

He drew one breath to the very bottom, and the warmth rode it and slammed into the gate.

There was a roar inside his head and a white flash, as if he had looked straight at the sun on a clear day. The warmth broke through, surged to the crown, turned over there, and came pouring down the front — forehead, bridge of the nose, throat, chest — like a canal with the sluice thrown open, back into the place below his navel, where it settled, steady.

Exactly one circle.

He opened his eyes.

The same thin cloud overhead, the same woodpile — and everything he saw was different. Every crack between the bricks of the court wall, he saw clearly; the veins on the wings of the cricket at the foot of the wall, clearly; three rooms away Sun Ergou muttering in his sleep, "Ma, I won't eat chaff," he heard plainly; next door in the kitchen, tomorrow's pickles were yesterday's, and a vat of rice had a corner gnawed by rats — he could smell that too.

He sat on the woodpile not daring to breathe, afraid that with one breath it would all be gone.

The token on his chest was hot as a flatbread fresh off the griddle.

A half-transparent little silver fox slipped out of the token and sat on his knee. It yawned, eyelids drooping, the very picture of not enough sleep, and said, "…Through, are you?"

Xiaoman stammered, "Th-through! Yinyue, in one night I —"

"I know," it said. "I planned it."

Xiaoman stopped short. "…Planned it?"

Yinyue yawned again. "You think you squatted there a whole year for nothing?"

Xiaoman was stunned. He thought a long while with his mouth open and said, "…Was it the marrow-washing pill?"

"The marrow pill was a chimney sweep," said Yinyue. "Your channels were clogged like the chimney over your family's stove — thirteen years of soot from bran and wild greens. One soak and it all came out. Remember that basin? Black enough to write with."

Xiaoman nodded. His mother had scrubbed that basin a whole morning and asked him nothing.

"But a clean chimney still has locked doors," said Yinyue. "There are three gates in your body, each tighter than the last. If you'd butted them yourself, the way you butt, you'd still be at it at thirty, and if you ever got them open you'd have butted yourself simple. So I slept at your heart —"

It lifted a paw and touched the small of his back, the middle of his back, the back of his head: "Weilü, Jiaji, Yuzhen. The Three Passes. Every night, while you breathed, I used my own qi to chisel them open for you, bit by bit. I chiselled two and a half. The last half you had to break yourself — if I'd broken it for you, you'd never in your life know how a gate opens."

Xiaoman sat with his mouth open and couldn't speak for a long time.

He thought of that winter at home, sitting on the woodpile every night breathing and getting nothing, a dry well under his belly. He had thought there was nothing there. He thought of how every night, after breathing, he would cup the token in his hands and give it the day's accounts, and afterwards the token was always warm. He had thought his palms had warmed it.

Three hundred and more nights he had sat on the woodpile thinking himself a dry well with nothing in it; and all along someone had been at the bottom of the well, digging for him.

After a good while he said, "…So I'm not a genius."

"You're a skimmer," said Yinyue. "I'm the tinker who mends pots."

Xiaoman burst out laughing — and halfway through he couldn't laugh any more. Only now did he look at it properly.

It was thinner than last time. Last time, in the lecture hall, it had only been a voice; the time before, last autumn, the night it slipped into the token, it had been thin as paper, and moonlight shone through it. Tonight there was no moon, only a little starlight, and even the starlight went through it; through its body he could see the woodpile behind, each pine log on the pile. Its single tail hung down over his knee, not even the tip lifting, and the eight cut stumps at its root were darker than last year.

He said, "…And you? You chiselled a whole year — you —"

Yinyue turned its face away. "I am a demon queen. What's chiselling a few gates."

Xiaoman said nothing, only looked at it.

It didn't look at him. It gazed at the dark mountains beyond the court wall, and after a while said low, "…Just means sleeping a few more days."

It paused, then turned back and flicked him a glance. "Also — that whole year you gave me accounts every night. How many buckets of water today, how many cakes Ma Xiaobao ate tomorrow. Noisy as anything."

Xiaoman went red. "You… heard it all?"

"I was asleep," said Yinyue, "not deaf."

After that it said no more, and neither did Xiaoman. Under the woodpile a cricket chirped twice and stopped. He thought of last autumn: the token cool, not warming, and he sitting on the woodpile till the moon went down. What he had said that night, he remembered exactly.

It had mentioned the water, and Ma Xiaobao's cakes, and not that one word. He opened his mouth to ask, and in the end did not.

refuse.zh: 那一口气还在门后头打转。——三关，你自己撞：一呼，一吸，等风歇一口气。
refuse.en: That breath is still circling behind the gate. — Break the Three Passes yourself: out, in, and wait for the wind to catch its breath.
